stories.headline: WTI CRUDE SURGES NEARLY 5% TO $82 AS STRAIT OF HORMUZ UNCERTAINTY RATTLES OIL MARKETS
stories.body: WTI crude jumped roughly 5% to settle near $82.13 a barrel and Brent rose to about $84 as traders weighed uncertainty over a reported U.S.-Iran agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for roughly a fifth of global oil flows. The rally reversed last week's calmer tape and fed straight into a broader risk-off tone across rate-sensitive assets.
stories.explain: About 20% of the world's seaborne crude passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so even a hint of disruption or a delayed reopening forces traders to price in a persistent supply risk premium rather than a one-day spike. Because energy carries an outsized weight in headline CPI, a sustained move to $82 WTI raises the odds that Wednesday's inflation print comes in hotter than the softer trend the June-July data implied, directly threatening the rate-cut narrative that powered last week's rally.

stories.headline: CLEVELAND FED'S HAMMACK PUSHES BACK ON RATE-CUT BETS, SAYS HIKES 'REMAIN NECESSARY'
stories.body: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack struck a hawkish tone Monday, arguing further rate hikes may still be needed even after Friday's weak July payrolls report, directly challenging the market's growing conviction that the Fed cuts in September. Fed funds futures trimmed the implied odds of a September cut following her remarks.
stories.explain: Hammack is a voting FOMC member this cycle, so her comments carry more weight for near-term policy than a non-voter's would, and traders adjust the probability distribution embedded in fed funds futures almost immediately. Her pushback matters because it reintroduces two-sided risk into a market that had priced Friday's jobs miss as a clean, one-directional signal toward easing — a reminder that one weak payrolls print doesn't guarantee a pivot if inflation data doesn't cooperate too.

stories.headline: TREASURY YIELDS CLIMB ACROSS THE CURVE AS MARKETS BRACE FOR WEDNESDAY'S CPI
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 4 bps to 4.71% and the 2-year added roughly 3 bps to 4.24%, unwinding a slice of Friday's post-jobs-report rally as traders repriced Fed expectations ahead of Wednesday's CPI release, the last major data point before the September FOMC meeting.
stories.explain: Both ends of the curve rose together today rather than the front end diverging, which signals the move is less about a shift in Fed-specific expectations and more a broad repricing of inflation risk following the oil spike — a parallel shift rather than the front-end-led steepening seen after Friday's payrolls miss. With CPI now the decisive data point, yields are effectively pricing a wider range of outcomes: a soft print resumes the rate-cut trade, while a hot one — made more likely by $82 oil — pushes the Fed back toward Hammack's hawkish camp.

stories.headline: S&P 500 SLIPS 0.06% TO 7,753, NASDAQ 100 DOWN 0.23% AS OIL SPIKE COOLS LAST WEEK'S RATE-CUT RALLY
stories.body: The S&P 500 closed at 7,753.11, down 0.06% off Friday's record, while the Nasdaq 100 fell about 0.23% to roughly 29,421 as the oil-driven inflation scare and Hammack's hawkish comments offset the dovish momentum from Friday's jobs report.
stories.explain: Equities are being squeezed by two forces pulling in opposite directions at once: a weak labor market that argues for lower discount rates, and a supply-driven oil spike that argues for higher realized inflation and a more hawkish Fed reaction function. When those forces roughly offset, as they did today, the index barely moves even though the underlying narrative shifted meaningfully — a flat headline number can still mask a real change in market expectations underneath.

stories.headline: FIRST SOLAR SLIDES 5.6% IN PROFIT-TAKING AFTER A 14% TARIFF-DRIVEN RALLY
stories.body: First Solar shares fell 5.6% Monday, giving back a chunk of a roughly 14% run-up sparked by recent tariff policy favoring domestic panel manufacturers, as investors locked in gains after the sharp move.
stories.explain: Tariff-driven rallies tend to be more fragile than earnings-driven ones because the underlying catalyst is a policy decision that can be reversed, litigated, or watered down through exemptions, so investors are quicker to take profits once the initial repricing plays out. The pullback is a useful reminder that a stock re-rating on trade policy reflects a shift in expected competitive dynamics, not a change in near-term fundamentals — which is exactly why these moves often partially round-trip once the news cycle moves on.

stories.headline: COURT INJUNCTION FORCES SURPRISE AUGUST TRANSFER PORTAL WINDOW, UPENDING ROSTERS LEAGUE-WIDE
stories.body: A federal judge's class-wide preliminary injunction is forcing the NCAA to restore a fifth season of eligibility to Division I players who began competing in 2022-23 and exhausted eligibility this spring, triggering a surprise transfer portal window that ran Aug. 3-10 and caught coaches off guard with rosters and budgets already set. The NCAA is expected to appeal.

stories.headline: DON NELSON, SECOND-WINNINGEST COACH IN NBA HISTORY, DIES AT 86
stories.body: Hall of Famer Don Nelson died Sunday, his family confirmed. He won five titles as a Celtics player before becoming the NBA's second-winningest coach ever, notching 250-plus wins with three different franchises (Milwaukee, Dallas, Golden State) while also serving as each team's GM and winning three Coach of the Year awards across 31 seasons.

stories.headline: FALCONS' JALON WALKER TEARS ACL IN CAMP, OUT FOR THE SEASON
stories.body: Atlanta's 2025 first-round pick (No. 15 overall) tore his ACL during an 11-on-11 camp drill and was carted off, ending his season before it starts. Walker posted 5.5 sacks as a rookie and was expected to anchor a leap forward for the Falcons' pass rush in 2026.

stories.headline: OHIO STATE OPENS NO. 1 IN 2026 PRESEASON COACHES POLL
stories.body: The AFCA Coaches Poll tabbed Ohio State No. 1 with 38 first-place votes — the Buckeyes' first preseason coaches' No. 1 since 2015 — with Oregon, Georgia, Texas and Notre Dame rounding out the top five behind Heisman contenders QB Julian Sayin and WR Jeremiah Smith. The AP Top 25 follows Aug. 17.

sports.detail: Fall camp rolls on with junior Jayvon Parker emerging as the first-team defensive tackle after returning from injury; both cornerback spots remain open (Ephesians Prysock/Elijah Jackson, Thaddeus Dixon/Darren Barkins) while LB Jamaal Kearse (tibia stress fracture) and James Johnson (dislocated wrist) work back. Season opener vs. Washington State (Apple Cup) is Sunday, Sept. 6, 1 PM PT on NBC.

Danny Sprinkle landed ex-USC point guard Desmond Claude, the top available transfer, plus Rutgers's Harun Zrno, filling out a 15-man roster with six portal additions after guards Courtland Muldrew, Zoom Diallo and JJ Mandaquit all left. Returners Wesley Yates III, Jasir Rencher and Nikola Dzepina anchor the group; Sprinkle also added 25-year NBA veteran Charles Klask to the staff.

Training camp continues at the VMAC ahead of Sunday's preseason opener vs. the Dallas Cowboys (Lumen Field, 5 PM PT, KING 5). The rest of the slate has Seattle at Tennessee (Aug. 23, national FOX window) before a finale at Kansas City.

Restricted free agent Jalen Duren remains unsigned well into August, seeking a five-year, roughly $287M extension after an All-NBA Third Team season, while Detroit resists a full max to preserve cap flexibility. No rival offer sheet has emerged to force the issue; Duren's fallback is a $9.6M qualifying offer and 2027 unrestricted free agency.

Fell 4-1 to Tampa Bay on Sunday, Aug. 9 at T-Mobile Park in a series-clinching sweep for the Rays; Ian Seymour tossed six innings of one-run ball and Cedric Mullins' fifth-inning RBI single proved the difference. Seattle sits a handful of games back of Houston in a tight AL West race. Next: at the Yankees, Tuesday, Aug. 11.

Mariners at Yankees — Tuesday, Aug. 11, 7:05 PM ET, Yankee Stadium — Seattle looks to snap a series skid in a tight AL West race

deepDive.title: Oil, CPI, and the Fed's Reaction Function: Why $82 Crude Complicates Wednesday's Inflation Print
content: Today's ~5% jump in WTI to $82 a barrel lands one week before the single most important data release on the Fed's calendar right now. Friday's weak payrolls report had markets leaning hard toward a September rate cut, but Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack's hawkish pushback and now a supply-driven oil shock both cut against that narrative on the same day. Wednesday's CPI print was already going to be the tie-breaker between those two competing stories; a fresh energy spike raises the stakes on which way it breaks.

The mechanism is direct: energy makes up roughly 6-7% of the headline CPI basket, split between motor fuel, electricity, and natural gas, and gasoline pump prices typically catch up to wholesale crude moves within one to three weeks as refiners and retailers pass through higher input costs. A jump from roughly $78 to $82 WTI this week is exactly the kind of move that shows up in the next one or two CPI reports' energy component, even before accounting for the diesel and jet-fuel costs that ripple into trucking, shipping, and air-travel prices — the indirect, second-round channel that hits core services with a longer lag.

The distinction the Fed actually cares about is headline versus core CPI, and it's easy to miss why. The Fed targets core (ex food and energy) specifically because oil shocks are frequently transitory — the 1990 Gulf War spike and the 2022 post-invasion surge both reversed within a year — so a single month's energy-driven headline print rarely changes the policy path on its own. What does matter is whether an oil shock bleeds into inflation expectations or wage-setting behavior, turning a temporary relative-price shift into persistent inflation; that contagion risk is precisely what a hawkish voter like Hammack is flagging preemptively.

For Wednesday, the read-through is that markets should watch the composition of the CPI print, not just the top-line number. A hot headline driven mostly by the energy component is a very different signal than hot core services or shelter inflation — the former argues the Fed can look through it, the latter validates Hammack's hawkishness and could push the September cut further out of reach. Given that both stocks and the bond market barely moved on net today despite yields, oil, and Fed rhetoric all shifting hawkish simultaneously, the market is effectively holding its breath for Wednesday's composition to resolve which story wins.
